summary: Defines the CDN-Loop HTTP request header field, used to detect and stop non-terminating request loops when a request is forwarded between content delivery networks and accidentally or maliciously sent back to the first. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: If two delivery companies keep passing a package back and forth, it never arrives. This header leaves a stamp so they can notice and stop.

questions: what is the cdn-loop http header
how do cdns detect forwarding loops
why not use the via header for loop detection
subtitle: A request header that lets a CDN notice when a request has come back around to it, so loops can be stopped.

tldr.problem: When requests are forwarded between Content Delivery Networks, a configuration mistake or an attack can send a request back into the first CDN and make it loop without end.
tldr.mechanism: Each participating CDN adds its own identifier to a new CDN-Loop request header field, and a CDN that sees its own identifier in an incoming request knows the request has looped.
tldr.outcome: The header only works if every intermediary keeps it and customers cannot edit or remove it. It is a Proposed Standard and is registered as a permanent header field.

facts.label: Identifier
facts.value: Hostname with optional port, or a pseudonym token

facts.label: Requirement to add
facts.value: SHOULD add in every request generated or forwarded

today: RFC 8586 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2019. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata, so it remains the definition of the CDN-Loop header.

sections.title: Why CDNs Can Loop
sections.content:
A Content Delivery Network (CDN) sits in front of an origin server to cut latency and cost and to improve scalability and reliability. Often one origin uses more than one CDN, for cost savings, for failover, or to compare the services directly.

Because routing depends on a mix of DNS and forwarding rules, often managed by several parties, CDNs can end up forwarding to each other in a loop by accident. Such loops are hard to debug. They are also sometimes deliberate: the RFC notes that loops between CDNs can be used as an attack vector, especially if one CDN unintentionally strips another CDN's loop detection headers.

RFC 8586 defines the CDN-Loop HTTP request header field to detect these cases among CDNs that implement it. Customers must not be able to modify the header field.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine two mail carriers who each think the other should deliver a letter, so it goes back and forth forever. Sometimes that happens by mistake, and sometimes someone does it on purpose to cause trouble.

sections.title: Why Not Use Via
sections.content:
HTTP already has a Via header field, defined in RFC 7230, for tracking message forwards, avoiding request loops and identifying the capabilities of senders along the chain. In theory it could find these loops.

In practice it is not used that way. Some HTTP servers use Via for other purposes, and in particular some implementations disable some HTTP/1.1 features when the header is present. A dedicated header avoids that problem.
sections.plainLanguage: There was already a general sign-in sheet for packages, but some offices change how they work when they see it. So a separate, special stamp is safer.

sections.title: The CDN-Loop Header Syntax
sections.content:
The header is a comma-separated list of cdn-info entries. Each entry is a cdn-id, optionally followed by semicolon-separated key/value parameters for the CDN's own use. The cdn-id is either a hostname (with an optional port) or a pseudonym, which is an HTTP token.

Hostnames under the CDN's control are preferred because they help avoid accidental collisions. A pseudonym is more likely to collide, so it should be chosen carefully: a well-known value such as the recognized name of the CDN, or a generated value with enough entropy, such as a UUID. The pseudonym syntax does not allow whitespace, double quotes or delimiter characters such as parentheses, commas, slashes, colons, semicolons and brackets.

As with other headers defined as comma-separated lists, a CDN can add its entry by comma-separating onto an existing value or by creating a new header field line.
sections.plainLanguage: Each company signs the package with its own name, or a secret nickname if it prefers. The name has to be unusual enough that nobody else uses the same one.

sections.title: What a CDN Does With It
sections.content:
Conforming CDNs SHOULD add a cdn-info to this header field in all requests they generate or forward, creating the header field if necessary. A CDN that receives a request already carrying its own identifier can conclude that the request has passed through its servers before, which means a loop.

The mechanism only works if all intermediaries preserve the header. Removing it, or letting a customer remove it through configuration, stops downstream CDNs from detecting looping. Unknown header fields are generally left alone by intermediaries, but implementations may need to add CDN-Loop to a list of fields that are never removed. The header field SHOULD NOT be used for other purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every company stamps each package it handles. If a company sees its own stamp already on a package that just arrived, it knows the package has gone in a circle and can stop it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The threat model is a customer attacking a service provider by configuring a forwarding loop, by accident or on purpose. For the defense to work, CDNs cannot let customers modify or remove the header in their configuration. A CDN that does allow this remains an attack vector against both implementing and non-implementing CDNs.

There are other cautions. Using the header might reveal that a CDN is present, for example if CDN B behaves differently when it sees the header from CDN A. Any client can generate the header, so its contents cannot be trusted, and a CDN that changes its behavior based on the contents must make sure that does not become an attack vector such as Denial of Service. Signing the contents is possible but not defined or required. Depending on use, the header can also expose internal details such as the number of hops inside a CDN and the hostnames of nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: The stamp only helps if customers cannot erase it. Also, anyone can fake a stamp, and a stamp can show which companies were involved, so companies should be careful what they trust and what they reveal.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The document registers the CDN-Loop header field in the Permanent Message Header Field Names registry. The protocol is http, the status is standard, and the reference is RFC 8586.
sections.plainLanguage: The new stamp was added to the official list of header names so nobody else picks the same name for something different.

data.title: A request with two CDN-Loop lines
data.code:
GET /image.jpg HTTP/1.1
Host: cdn-customer.example
User-Agent: ExampleBrowser/5
CDN-Loop: foo123.foocdn.example, barcdn.example; trace="abcdef"
CDN-Loop: AnotherCDN; abc=123; def="456"
